problem: Interactive imitation learning needs explicit, hand-defined intervention criteria (state novelty, task-performance thresholds) that generalize poorly, and autonomous navigation policies fail in unfamiliar environments (getting stuck, wasteful exploration).
motivation: Data collection and model refinement cannot be done in every deployment environment, and full teleoperation is expensive. A robot that knows when to ask for help can recover from mistakes with only part-time human input. The paper observes that uncertainty in the frozen navigation policy's visual features can serve as an implicit signal for when a human helps most.
key_idea: Train a lightweight MLP interaction policy with PPO on top of a frozen point-nav policy's encoder features and goal vector, with a reward that penalizes human requests in proportion to implicit uncertainty (1 - |P(ask) - P(proceed)|) and current interaction ratio.
insight: Success rises roughly linearly with interaction rate for the best policy (xi>=1), which suggests requests concentrate at points where the agent benefits (stuck at tight obstacles, dead ends, wasteful exploration). The lambda_h ablation shows the trade-off: 0.0 gives SR 0.959 at 0.714 interaction, 0.5 gives the best efficiency (1.277), and 1.0 gives SR 0.622 at 0.126. The policy transfers zero-shot to a new domain because it relies on generic features rather than explicit task state, though the transfer evidence is small (14 episodes).
method: Frozen autonomous policy: Habitat baseline PointNav actor-critic (ResNet18 RGB encoder + goal vector, GRU actor), pretrained on MP3D, 52.3% SR on HM3D.
Interaction policy: MLP on the frozen visual embedding and point-goal, outputting a distribution over proceed autonomously (a_r) or ask for help (a_h), trained with PPO.
Implicit uncertainty: certainty c_t = |P(a_h) - P(a_r)|, uncertainty = 1 - c_t.
Reward: success reward + hyperbolically discounted cumulative distance reward (lambda_d=0.9) minus an interaction penalty lambda_h*(1-c_t)*h_t/(h_t+a_t) applied only when help is requested.
Simulated expert: a shortest-path planner supplies actions during training (250k steps, ~1500 episodes on MP3D); evaluated on HM3D val.
Real human interface: GUI with agent view (red border autonomous, blue border for interaction), goal, distance and interaction stats, joystick control, used in FlightGoggles (Stata Center).

setting.backbone: Habitat PointNav actor-critic (ResNet18 + GRU, frozen) + MLP interaction policy (PPO)
setting.model_size: ResNet18-based nav policy; interaction policy is a small MLP
setting.training_data: Nav policy pretrained on MP3D (Habitat baseline); interaction policy trained with RL on MP3D for 250k steps (~1500 episodes) with shortest-path-planner expert; no extra data
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: turn_left, turn_right, move_forward, stop (plus a binary ask-for-help decision)

setting.privileged: Expert help: shortest-path planner (simulated human, i.e. GT map access) in Habitat; a real human expert in FlightGoggles

numbers_note: Autonomous baseline on HM3D val: SR 0.523, SPL 0.426. No standard SPL is reported for FlightGoggles. Metrics are given as fractions in the paper and converted to percent here except for interaction rate and efficiency.
results: With lambda_h=0.5 the interaction policy raises HM3D-val success from 0.523 to 0.906 (+0.38) and SPL from 0.426 to 0.786 at a 0.30 interaction rate. Zero-shot in FlightGoggles with a real human, success goes from 0.07-0.09 (autonomous) to 0.929 at a 0.232 interaction rate.
limitations: Requires manual control hand-off, so the human must pay close attention; no natural-language help or human-subject study of interface design.
The real-human evaluation is tiny (14 episodes, one simulated building) and the training expert is a shortest-path planner, not a human.
The base nav policy is not improved from the interactions, and only RGB PointNav is tested; no comparison with other intervention-triggering baselines.
